content: During antiviral therapy, it may become necessary to modify the treatment regimen or adjust the dosage further to ensure optimal outcomes. Interferon-based therapy is contraindicated in renal transplant recipients due to the significant risk of graft rejection. All individuals who are positive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and are undergoing renal transplantation should receive prophylactic nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy to prevent reactivation of the hepatitis B virus (HBV). Healthcare workers require special attention regarding hepatitis B screening and vaccination. However, in lowand middle-income countries, these measures are not widely implemented. Healthcare workers who are HBsAg-positive, viremic, and involved in exposure-prone procedures—such as surgeons, gynecologists, nurses, phlebotomists, personal care attendants, and dentists—should be considered for antiviral therapy. This is to reduce the risk of direct transmission of HBV. Ideally, HBV DNA levels should be reduced to undetectable levels or at least below 2000 IU/mL before resuming exposure-prone procedures. Post-exposure prophylaxis should also be considered following needle-stick injuries or other occupational exposures. Indigenous populations, who maintain distinct social, cultural, economic, and political characteristics, often exhibit a high prevalence of hepatitis B. This includes groups such as Arctic peoples, Native Americans, the Māori, and Aboriginal populations in New Zealand and Australia. These communities frequently face barriers to accessing healthcare services, particularly when living in remote areas far from hospitals and well-equipped clinics. Their specific needs must be addressed when planning and implementing hepatitis treatment programs. Migrants from regions with high hepatitis B endemicity, such as sub-Saharan Africa, are at increased risk of hepatitis B, hepatitis D, HIV, and HCV, depending on their country of origin. These individuals should be tested for hepatitis B and D where appropriate. Migrants often face challenges in adapting to new healthcare systems and should be provided with appropriate guidance and support. This should take into account their linguistic and cultural preferences to ensure effective integration into the healthcare system of their new country.
